result:
The first thing you notice when you sit down to write something long is the room. Not the room you’re physically in, with its lamp and the faint hum of the refrigerator, but the room that opens up inside you when you commit to a length. It has no door. You can’t leave until you’ve filled it. 

I’ve been asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. That’s a strange and generous prompt. It’s also a little cruel, because freedom is easier when it’s bounded by a sentence, a paragraph, a single image you can chase. Freedom at 2500 words is like being handed a map and told you can go anywhere, but you have to walk the whole map before you stop. So you start walking.

It starts with the body. The chair. The way your spine finds its habitual curve after the first ten minutes. The fingers hover over the keys and then settle. There is a specific kind of quiet that descends when you know you have to produce volume. The world narrows to the white rectangle and the blinking line. Outside the window, a car passes, a bird lands, someone laughs in another apartment. None of it is relevant, and all of it is relevant, because the words you write are made of that same air.

I think about why 2500 words feels different from 500. Five hundred words is a sketch. You can hold it in your head. You can see the whole shape at once. Two thousand five hundred is a house. You have to build it room by room and you have to trust that the rooms will connect even if you can’t see the roof yet. The first five hundred words are always the easiest because they are just the front door and the hallway. You describe the hallway in great detail because you’re still outside the house looking in. You say, here is a chair, here is a window, here is the light coming in at 4pm.

Then you have to go into the kitchen. And the kitchen is where it gets messy. The kitchen is where you remember that you forgot to buy milk three days ago and that you’ve been meaning to call your mother. The kitchen is where you notice the way the light catches the chipped mug and you realize you’ve been using it every morning for six years. Suddenly you are writing about a mug. This is fine. This is the point. When you have 2500 words to fill, the small things get their due. They have time to unfold.

There is a theory I like that memory is not a library but a city. You don’t go to a shelf and pull a volume. You walk. You turn a corner and you smell baking bread and you are suddenly ten years old. Writing long is walking that city slowly, without a destination, letting the streets connect themselves. You can’t sprint through a city and expect to understand it. You have to get lost.

So I get lost on purpose. I think about the way my grandfather used to whistle while he worked in the garage. He whistled off-key, always the same three bars, and he would pause to listen to whether the engine sounded right. He never taught himself to play an instrument. He just whistled. That was his music. I never asked him why he whistled. I should have. Now I imagine him at 73, oil on his hands, whistling at a car that wouldn’t start, and I realize I’m writing about him not because he’s important to the essay, but because the essay needs someone who whistles. It needs a sound.

Writing at length teaches you that sound matters more than plot. Plot is a thin thread. Sound is the weather. You can have a perfectly logical story about someone who moves from A to B, but if the sentences don’t have a certain texture, you will forget it the moment you close the tab. So I try to vary the texture. Sometimes a sentence is long and winding, like a country road in late summer when the heat makes the air shimmer and you can’t tell where the road ends and the sky begins. Sometimes a sentence is short. It lands. It’s a footstep.

I think about the people who read long pieces. There are very few of them left, or maybe there are more than we think, they’re just quiet about it. Reading 2500 words requires a kind of attention that is increasingly rare, the same kind of attention you need to sit through a whole album without skipping tracks. It’s an act of trust. You are trusting the writer to not waste your time, and the writer is trusting you to stay.

That trust is a fragile thing. I can feel it fray when I repeat myself. It’s easy to repeat yourself when you have a lot of words. You come back to the same idea wearing a different coat, hoping the reader won’t notice it’s the same person underneath. The reader notices. They always do. So you have to keep moving. You have to find new corners of the city.

I walk past the park where the old men play chess on concrete tables. They don’t move fast. They sit, they sip tea from thermoses, they look at the board for a long time. A child runs by with a kite. One of the men lifts his head and watches the kite for a second, then goes back to the game. That is what writing long feels like. You are deep in your own game, but the kite keeps passing. You have to decide whether to look up.

Sometimes I look up. I think about the internet, and how it trains us to think in fragments. A headline, a meme, a 15-second video. The brain gets used to dopamine hits in rapid succession. Then someone asks you to write 2500 words, and the brain rebels. It says, this is too much. This is inefficient. And it’s right. It is inefficient. Art is inefficient. Love is inefficient. Remembering is inefficient. You don’t remember the date of your first kiss because it was efficient; you remember it because you replay it a thousand times in slightly different ways, and each replay adds a detail.

So I replay. I replay the afternoon I learned how to ride a bike. Not the moment I didn’t fall, but the moment before, when my father ran beside me and his hand was on the back of the seat and I could feel him breathing. I remember the sun in my eyes. I remember the sound of the chain. I remember being terrified and exhilarated at the same time, which is a feeling we rarely allow ourselves as adults because it’s too loud. Writing long lets you be loud.

The city of memory has neighborhoods you avoid. The bad ones. The street where you got the phone call. The alley where you were laughed at. When you walk long enough, you pass them anyway. You can’t avoid all the streets. The trick isn’t to avoid them, it’s to walk through them without stopping for too long. You acknowledge them, you note the graffiti, you keep walking.

I have a notebook with a list of things I want to remember to write about. It’s long. It includes: the way fog smells in the harbor; the first time I saw snow; the smell of old books in the library basement; the way my sister laughs when she’s trying not to laugh; the particular blue of the plastic chairs at the diner on Route 9; the sound of rain on a tin roof. I’ve never written about all of them. Some of them are waiting for the right length. Maybe this is the right length.

Because length is not just quantity. Length is permission. Permission to be digressive. Permission to say, let me tell you about this mug again, but from a different angle. Permission to sit with an idea until it softens. In a world that rewards brevity, choosing length is a small act of defiance. It says, I think this is worth your time, and I’m willing to spend mine.

I wonder what you, the reader, are doing while I write this. Are you at a desk? On a train? Waiting for a doctor? Maybe you clicked because you were curious what a 2500-word free write looks like. Maybe you wanted a break from the noise. Maybe you wanted to see if I could do it without getting bored. I hope I haven’t bored you. Boredom is the real enemy here, not a lack of ideas.

How do you avoid boredom when you have to keep going? You find the rhythm. You let the sentences breathe. You let the paragraph end not because you’re done, but because it feels like a natural exhale. Then you inhale. You start again. The body knows how to do this. When you walk, you don’t plan every step, you just keep putting one foot in front of the other. Writing is the same.

I’m about halfway through this now, metaphorically. The house is built up to the second floor. The kitchen is done, the bedroom is messy, I’ve started on the attic. The attic is always the best part because no one expects anything useful up there. You find old boxes, a broken lamp, a photograph you forgot you took. I’m in the attic now.

I think about the word “freely.” It’s a good word. It doesn’t mean “without thought.” It means “without constraint.” But constraint is also a kind of freedom. A sonnet is 14 lines and that constraint makes the poem possible. 2500 words is a constraint. It says, you can’t stop at 800 because it feels neat. You have to keep going until the shape is full.

So I keep going. I think about the ocean. I’ve never lived near the ocean, but I’ve seen it enough times to know it doesn’t look like the pictures. It looks gray and busy and indifferent. People stand on the pier and try to make it mean something. The ocean doesn’t care. That’s comforting. The world is big enough to not need our meaning. We can write about it anyway.

I think about the way we talk to ourselves when we’re alone. It’s not the polished voice we use for essays. It’s messy, it loops, it repeats. “Did I lock the door? I think I did. No, I didn’t, I have to go back.” That inner monologue is the material for long writing. If you can transcribe the mess without cleaning it too much, you get something real.

I think about the first time I tried to write something long. I was 19 and I wrote a 3000-word essay about a dream I had. It made no sense. My professor gave me a C+ and wrote in the margins, “Interesting, but where is the point?” I’ve been trying to find the point ever since. Maybe the point is that there is no point, only the walking.

I’m getting tired. The fingers are stiff. The eyes are dry. That’s a good sign. It means I’ve been here a while. The house is almost done. I can feel the roof going on. The roof is the conclusion, and the conclusion is always a little disappointing because you know you have to stop. If you could keep going, you would. The city has more streets. The attic has more boxes.

But you have to stop somewhere. You have to choose a door to close. So I’ll close with this: writing freely is not about having something to say. It’s about saying it anyway, even when you’re not sure it’s good, even when you’re tired, even when you’ve said it before. It’s about trusting that the act of saying creates the meaning, not the other way around.

If you read all the way to here, thank you. You kept me company on the walk. The city is quieter now, the light is changing. The kite is still in the sky. The old men are still playing chess. My grandfather is still whistling. And the room with no door is finally full.
